title: Unplugging
hookLine: many put away phones and screens for the day
tomorrow: walk slowly on Shabbat, or run? two teachings disagree.

cards: Sunday morning, the phone posts its weekly screen-time report, and the number is rarely smaller than hoped. Now a puzzle. The Torah says don't work on the Sabbath.
It never mentions phones, screens, or anything with a battery. So why do some Jews put their phones in a drawer from Friday sunset until Saturday night?
The answer starts somewhere strange: in the middle of a set of building instructions.

teach.b: Exodus spends chapters on the Mishkan, the portable sanctuary in the desert: boards, curtains, gold, oil. And right in the middle of the instructions, it stops to say: keep the Sabbath. Then the building resumes.
The rabbis read that placement as a clue.
The kinds of work it took to build the sanctuary are the work you rest from on the seventh day. The Hebrew word is melakhah.
The Mishnah lists its kinds, forty less one: sowing, kneading, weaving, writing, building, lighting a fire, carrying from one domain to another. Notice what the list is about. Not sweat.
Making, shaping, changing the world. Six days a week people do that, the way God does in Genesis. On the seventh they stop, the way God does.
And the commandment hands the day off to the whole household: children, workers, the stranger, even the animals. Nobody in the house is on call. Now the phone.
In Orthodox practice, switching devices on and off counts as forbidden work, so the phone stays off.

teach.h: A PHONE IS A POCKET WORKSHOP.
teach.b: Jews who don't keep that law sometimes unplug anyway, by choice, because a phone is a pocket-size workshop: buying, posting, replying, fixing.
One to tell a friend tonight: Abraham Joshua Heschel called the Sabbath a palace in time, a building you enter by stopping.
Puzzle solved. The Torah didn't have to name the phone. It named what the phone does.

how: Jews who keep Shabbat by traditional law leave phones and screens off from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall; others choose a phone-free stretch of the day as rest, often keeping the device in a drawer or another room.

o: a short digital detox to sharpen your focus
resting a day from making and changing the world
switching off devices to save on electricity

games.q: the puzzle of the phone — tap the pairs.
p: the work of making and changing
forty less one kinds of work

s: the Torah forbids phones on the Sabbath in so many words
it never mentions them; the practice comes from melakhah, the work of making and changing.
the Mishnah's list of Sabbath work includes writing and lighting a fire
Mishnah Shabbat 7:2, forty less one kinds of work.
Sabbath work means anything that makes you tired
melakhah is about making and shaping, the kinds of work that built the sanctuary, not sweat.

games.q: your cousin keeps Shabbat. she'll read a paper book all afternoon, but won't scroll the same news on a tablet. same words, so why the difference?
o: the tablet switches on and changes things; the book just sits open.
screens strain the eyes, so the rabbis ruled them out.
the news is the problem, whatever it's printed on.
games.why: in Orthodox practice, switching a device on and off counts as melakhah, work that changes the world. turning a paper page doesn't.

practice: Choose your hours: a stretch of this coming Shabbat, or of any day this week, when the phone goes in a drawer, screen down, out of reach. Decide now where it will sit, and who should know you'll be off.
Then let your hands rest empty in your lap and notice what they want to reach for.

wordCard.voice: Unplugging: resting from melakhah, the work of making and changing the world, so the phone goes quiet too.

orig.note: Hebrew: work, the making kind. the kinds of work the Sabbath rests from, learned from building the Mishkan.

carryVoice: For today: unplugged, not punished, just off duty from changing the world for a day. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Exodus 31:12-17; Exodus 35:1-3 (the Sabbath set within the building of the Mishkan)
Mishnah Shabbat 7:2 (the primary kinds of work, forty less one)
Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 49b (the kinds of work correspond to the work of the Mishkan)
